question: Which of the UK-born individuals who won The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences while being affiliated with a UK based institution, between the inception of the award and the year that the first woman won The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, has fewer than 20 "Articles" listed on ideas.repec.org that have a publication year prior to the year that they won the award?

**Original Question:**
Which of the UK-born individuals who won The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences while being affiliated with a UK based institution, between the inception of the award and the year that the first woman won The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, has fewer than 20 "Articles" listed on ideas.repec.org that have a publication year prior to the year that they won the award?

**Previous Reasoning Steps:**
[turn 1] We need to find UK-born individuals who won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences while affiliated with a UK-based institution, between inception (1969) and the year the first woman won the prize. First woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was Esther Duflo? Actually the first woman was Esther Duflo? Let's recall: Economic Sciences Nobel winners: 1979: Milton Friedman, etc. The first woman is Esther Duflo? Wait Esther Duflo won 2019. But earlier a woman, maybe Barbara McClintock? No. Let's check: The first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics: Esther Duflo 2019. So the cutoff is 2018 (year before 2019). So we need UK-born prize winners from 1969-2018 inclusive, with affiliation to UK-based institution at time of award, and who are UK-born. Then check each of those individuals' number of Articles on ideas.repec.org with publication year prior to award year; if fewer than 20, then list those individuals.

We need to find list of UK-born winners. Known UK-born winners: Kenneth Arrow (born in Chicago? No), no. Lord J. David Thomas? Let's recall: winners include: 1968 was Harold H. Williams? Actually 1969: Sir William John Kingdon? Let's search. Instead, we can find list of Nobel laureates in Economics: Usually inclusive: 1969 Lewis R.... Let's search web.

[turn 2] We need list of UK-born individuals who won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, who were affiliated with a UK-based institution at time of award, between inception (1969) and year when first woman won the prize.

First woman: Claudia Goldin, 2021? Actually first female winner of Nobel in Economic Sciences is economist Claudia Goldin, 2021 Nobel Prize. Wait: earlier female laureate is 1953? But Economic Sciences started 1969; before that no award. Women winners: 2021 Claudia Goldin is first woman. So timeframe: 1969-2020 inclusive.

UK-born individuals: Must be born in UK. Affiliated with UK-based institution at award. Need those who won between 1969-2020, UK-born, affiliation UK. Identify list.

Let's search.

[turn 3] We need: UK-born individuals who won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences while being affiliated with a UK-based institution. And between inception of award (1969) and year first woman won (2010? Actually first woman awarded 2010: Elinor Ostrom). So we consider winners from 1969 to 2009 inclusive. Among those winners, we need UK-born and affiliation with UK institution at time of award. Then out of those individuals, find who has fewer than 20 Articles listed on ideas.repec.org that have publication year prior to the year they won. We need identify all such candidates and then find those with less than 20 articles before win.

Thus steps:

1. List all Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences winners 1969-2009.
2. Identify UK-born winners (born in UK or UK-born nationality).
3. Note their affiliation at time of award - must be UK-based institution.
4. Then for each, count articles on ideas.repec.org with publication year < win year (so earlier than win year). Count if fewer than 20.

We need evidence for each candidate that answers conditions.

Let's find list with birth place and affiliation. Wikipedia page of each laureate can contain info. Could use "List of Nobel Memorial Prize laureates in Economic Sciences" page. Let's inspect that page.

The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").

The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne_), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)

The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-7)

As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").

The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne_), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)

The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-7)

As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").

The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne_), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)

The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-7)

As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

John R. Hicks  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1972

Born: 8 April 1904, Warwick, United Kingdom

Died: 20 May 1989, Blockley, United Kingdom

Affiliation at the time of the award: All Souls College, Oxford, United Kingdom

Prize motivation: “for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

John Hicks was born in Warwick, UK. He studied mathematics, philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford University. From 1926-35, Hicks lectured at the London School of Economics and Political Science. He also taught at Cambridge University and the University of Manchester before returning to Oxford in 1946. Hicks married Ursula Webb in 1935.

### Work

John Hicks made pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory. In his work Value and Capital (1939), Hicks presented a complete economic equilibrium model with aggregated markets for commodities, factors of production, credit and money. Hick’s model became of great importance as connecting a link between general equilibrium theory and theories of business cycles.

 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1972

Born: 8 April 1904, Warwick, United Kingdom

Died: 20 May 1989, Blockley, United Kingdom

Affiliation at the time of the award: All Souls College, Oxford, United Kingdom

Prize motivation: “for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

John Hicks was born in Warwick, UK. He studied mathematics, philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford University. From 1926-35, Hicks lectured at the London School of Economics and Political Science. He also taught at Cambridge University and the University of Manchester before returning to Oxford in 1946. Hicks married Ursula Webb in 1935.

### Work

John Hicks made pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory. In his work Value and Capital (1939), Hicks presented a complete economic equilibrium model with aggregated markets for commodities, factors of production, credit and money. Hick’s model became of great importance as connecting a link between general equilibrium theory and theories of business cycles.

**Ronald Harry Coase** ([/k oʊ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); 29 December 1910 – 2 September 2013) was a British economist and author. Coase was educated at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"), where he was a member of the faculty until 1951. He was the Clifton R. Musser Professor of Economics at the [University of Chicago Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Law_School "University of Chicago Law School"), where he arrived in 1964 and remained for the rest of his life. He received the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in 1991.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-1)

Coase believed economists should study real-world wealth creation, in the manner of [Adam Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Smith "Adam Smith"), stating, "It is suicidal for the field to slide into a hard science of choice, ignoring the influences of society, history, culture, and politics on the working of the economy."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-2) He believed economic study should reduce emphasis on [price theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_theory "Price theory") or theoretical markets and instead focus on real markets.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:1-4) He established the case for the corporation as a means to pay the costs of operating a marketplace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:0-3) Coase is best known for two articles: "[The Nature of the Firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nature_of_the_Firm "The Nature of the Firm")" (1937), which introduces the concept of [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") to explain the nature and limits of [firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation"); and "[The Problem of Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Problem_of_Social_Cost "The Problem of Social Cost")" (1960), which suggests that well-defined [property rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_rights_(economics) "Property rights (economics)") could overcome the problems of [externalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externalities "Externalities") if it were not for transaction costs (see [Coase theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem "Coase theorem")). Additionally, Coase's transaction costs approach has been influential in modern [organizational economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizational_economics "Organizational economics"), where it was re-introduced by [Oliver E. Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_E._Williamson "Oliver E. Williamson").

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg/250px-Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg)

Ronald Coase

Ronald Harry Coase was born in [Willesden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willesden "Willesden"), a suburb of London, on 29 December 1910. His father, Henry Joseph Coase (1884–1973) was a [telegraphist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraphist "Telegraphist") for the post office, as was his mother, Rosalie Elizabeth Coase (née Giles; 1882–1972), before marriage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-International-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-7) As a child, Coase had a weakness in his legs, for which he was required to wear [leg-irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brace_(orthopaedic) "Brace (orthopaedic)"). Due to this problem, he attended the school for physical defectives. At the age of 12, he was able to enter [Kilburn Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilburn_Grammar_School "Kilburn Grammar School") on scholarship. At Kilburn, he studied for the intermediate examination of the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") as an [external student](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London_International_Programmes "University of London International Programmes") in 1927–29.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-Coase_Autobiography-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-9)

Coase then continued his studies at the University of London, enrolling as an internal student of the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"), where he took courses with [Arnold Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Plant "Arnold Plant")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-Coase_Autobiography-8) and received a [Bachelor of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Commerce "Bachelor of Commerce") degree in 1932. During his undergraduate studies, Coase received the Sir Ernest Cassel Travelling Scholarship which he used to visit the University of Chicago in 1931–1932 studying with [Frank Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Knight "Frank Knight") and [Jacob Viner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Viner "Jacob Viner"). Coase's colleagues would later admit that they did not remember this first visit.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-FireofTruth-10) Between 1932 and 1934, Coase was an assistant lecturer at the Dundee School of Economics and Commerce, which later became part of the [University of Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Dundee "University of Dundee"). Subsequently, Coase was an assistant lecturer in commerce at the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") between 1934 and 1935 before returning to [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") as a member of staff until 1951 in which year he was awarded an earned doctorate in economics from the University of London. He then started to work at the [University at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York") and retained his British citizenship after moving to the United States in the 1950s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-11) In 1958, he moved to the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia"). Coase settled at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") in 1964 and became the co-editor of the _[Journal of Law and Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal\_of\_Law\_and\_Economics "Journal of Law and Economics")_ with [Aaron Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Director "Aaron Director").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-12) He was also for a time a trustee of the [Philadelphia Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Society "Philadelphia Society").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-13) He received the [Nobel Prize in Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Economics "Nobel Prize in Economics") in 1991.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_%281910%E2%80%932013%29_at_Graceland_Cemetery%2C_Chicago.jpg/250px-Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_%281910%E2%80%932013%29_at_Graceland_Cemetery%2C_Chicago.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_(1910%E2%80%932013)_at_Graceland_Cemetery,_Chicago.jpg)

Ronald Harry Coase's grave at [Graceland Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graceland_Cemetery "Graceland Cemetery"). The epitaph reads: "Here Sleeps in Peace RONALD H. COASE 1910 - 2013 Devoted husband and single-minded economist, whose ideas have inspired the great transformation of China and will continue to inspire our inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations."

Nearing his 100th birthday, Coase was working on a book concerning the rise of the economies of China and Vietnam.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-14) In an interview, Coase explained the mission of the Coase China Society and his vision of economics and the part to be played by Chinese economists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-16) This became "How China Became Capitalist" (2012) co-authored with Ning Wang. Coase was honoured and received an honorary doctorate from the university at Buffalo Department of Economics in May 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-17)

Coase married Marian Ruth Hartung of Chicago, Illinois in Willesden, England, 7 August 1937.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-International-6) Although they were unable to have children, they were married 75 years until her death on 17 October 2012, making him one of the longest-married Nobel Prize laureates.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:1-4)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-NYT-18) Coase himself died in Chicago on 2 September 2013, at the age of 102.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-19) Both are buried at [Graceland Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graceland_Cemetery "Graceland Cemetery") in Chicago.

He was praised across the political spectrum, with _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ calling him "one of the most distinguished economists in the world"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-slate-20) and _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ calling him "the greatest of the many great University of Chicago economists".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-forbes-21)_[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ called his work over eight decades "impossible to summarize" while recommending five of his papers to read.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-wapo-22)

## Contributions to economics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contributions to economics")]

### "The Nature of the Firm"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: \"The Nature of the Firm\"")]

Main article: [The Nature of the Firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nature_of_the_Firm "The Nature of the Firm")

In "The Nature of the Firm" (1937), a brief but highly influential essay, Coase attempts to explain why the economy features a number of [business firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation") instead of consisting exclusively of a multitude of independent, self-employed people who contract with one another. Given that "production could be carried on without any organization [that is, firms] at all", Coase asks, why and under what conditions should we expect firms to emerge?

Since modern firms can only emerge when an entrepreneur of some sort begins to hire people, Coase's analysis proceeds by considering the conditions under which it makes sense for an entrepreneur to seek hired help instead of contracting out for some particular task.

The traditional economic theory of the time (in the tradition of [Adam Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Smith "Adam Smith")) suggested that, because the market is "efficient" (that is, those who are best at providing each good or service most cheaply are already doing so), it should always be cheaper to contract out than to hire.

Coase noted, however, a number of [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") involved in using the market; the cost of obtaining a good or service via the market actually exceeds the price of the good. Other costs, including search and information costs, bargaining costs, keeping [trade secrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_secret "Trade secret"), and policing and enforcement costs, can all potentially add to the cost of procuring something from another party. This suggests that firms will arise which can internalise the production of goods and services required to deliver a product, thus avoiding these costs. This argument sets the stage for the later contributions by [Oliver Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Williamson "Oliver Williamson"): markets and hierarchies are alternative co-ordination mechanisms for economic transactions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-24)

There is a natural limit to what a firm can produce internally, however. Coase notices "decreasing returns to the entrepreneur function", including increasing [overhead costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_expenses "Overhead expenses") and increasing propensity for an overwhelmed manager to make mistakes in resource allocation. These factors become countervailing costs to the use of the firm.

Coase argues that the size of a firm (as measured by how many contractual relations are "internal" to the firm and how many "external") is a result of finding an optimal balance between the competing tendencies of the costs outlined above. In general, making the firm larger will initially be advantageous, but the decreasing returns indicated above will eventually kick in, preventing the firm from growing indefinitely.

Other things being equal, therefore, a firm will tend to be larger:

*   the lower the costs of organising and the slower these costs rise with an increase in the number of transactions organised
*   the less likely the entrepreneur is to make mistakes and the smaller the increase in mistakes with an increase in the transactions organised
*   the greater the lowering (or the smaller the rise) in the supply price of factors of production to firms of larger size

The first two costs will increase with the spatial distribution of the transactions organised and the dissimilarity of the transactions. This explains why firms tend to either be in different geographic locations or to perform different functions. Additionally, technology changes that mitigate the cost of organising transactions across space may allow firms to become larger – the advent of the telephone and of cheap air travel, for example, would be expected to increase the size of firms.

A further exploration of the dichotomy between markets and hierarchies as co-ordination mechanisms for economic transactions derived a third alternative way called [Commons based peer production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commons_based_peer_production "Commons based peer production"), in which individuals successfully collaborate on large-scale projects following a diverse cluster of motivational drives and social signals.

### "The Problem of Social Cost"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"The Problem of Social Cost\"")]

Main article: [The Problem of Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Problem_of_Social_Cost "The Problem of Social Cost")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Coase_working_2000s.jpg/250px-Coase_working_2000s.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_working_2000s.jpg)

Coase at the University of Chicago Law School in 2003

Upon publishing his article The Federal Communications Commission in 1959, Coase received negative feedback from the faculty at the University of Chicago over his conclusions and apparent conflicts with [A.C. Pigou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Cecil_Pigou "Arthur Cecil Pigou"). According to Coase, "What I said was thought to run counter to Pigou's analysis by a number of economists at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") and was therefore, according to them, wrong. At a meeting in Chicago I was able to convince these economists that I was right and Pigou's analysis faulty." Coase had presented his paper in 1960 during a seminar in Chicago, to twenty senior economist including [George Stigler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stigler "George Stigler") and [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman "Milton Friedman"). He gradually won over the usually skeptic audience, in what has later been considered a "paradigm-shifting moment" in the genesis of Chicago Law and Economics.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-25) Coase would join the Chicago faculty four years later.

Published in the _Journal of Law and Economics_ in 1960, while Coase was a member of the Economics department at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia"), "The Problem of [Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Cost "Social Cost")" provided the key insight that it is unclear where the blame for externalities lies. The example he gave was of a rancher whose cattle stray onto the cropland of his neighbour. If the rancher is made to restrict his cattle, he is harmed just as the farmer is if the cattle remain unrestrained.

Coase argued that without [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") the initial assignment of property rights makes no difference to whether or not the farmer and rancher can achieve the economically efficient outcome. If the cost of restraining cattle by, say, building a fence, is less than the cost of crop damage, the fence will be built. The initial assignment of property rights determines who builds the fence. If the farmer is responsible for the crop damage, the farmer will pay for the fence (as long the fence costs less than the crop damage). The allocation of property rights is primarily an equity issue, with consequences for the distribution of income and wealth, rather than an efficiency issue.

With sufficient transaction costs, initial property rights matter for both equity and efficiency. From the point of view of economic efficiency, property rights should be assigned such that the owner of the rights wants to take the economically efficient action. To elaborate, if it is efficient not to restrict the cattle, the rancher should be given the rights (so that cattle can move about freely), whereas if it is efficient to restrict the cattle, the farmer should be given the rights over the movement of the cattle (so the cattle are restricted).

This seminal argument forms the basis of the famous [Coase theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem "Coase theorem") as labelled by Stigler. In 1990, Coase wrote that he feared "The Problem of Social Cost" had been widely misunderstood.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-26)

### Law and economics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Law and economics")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Coase_profile_2003.jpg/250px-Coase_profile_2003.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_profile_2003.jpg)

Coase at the University of Chicago Law School

Though trained as an economist, Coase spent much of his career working in a law school. He is a central figure in the development of the subfield of [law and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_and_economics "Law and economics"). He viewed law and economics as having two parts, the first "using the economists' approach and concepts to analyze the working of the legal system, often called the economic analysis of the law"; and the second "a study of the influence of the legal system on the working of the economic system."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27) Coase said that the second part "is the part of law and economics in which I am most interested."

In his Simons Lecture celebrating the centennial of the University of Chicago, titled "Law and Economics at Chicago", Coase noted that he only accidentally wandered into the field:

> It is generally agreed that this article has had an immense influence on legal scholarship, but this was no part of my intention. For me, 'The Problem of Social Cost' was an essay in economics. It was aimed at economists. What I wanted to do was to improve our analysis of the working of the economic system. Law came into article because, in a regime of positive transaction costs, the character of the law becomes one of the main factors determining the performance of the economy. If transaction costs were zero (as is assumed in standard economic theory) we can imagine people contracting around the law whenever the value of production would be increased by a change in the legal position. But in a regime of positive transaction costs, such contracting would not occur whenever transaction costs were greater than the gain that such a redistribution of rights would bring. As a consequence the rights which individuals possess will commonly be those established by the law, which in these circumstances can be said to control the economy. As I have said, in 'The Problem of Social Cost' I had no intention of making a contribution to legal scholarship. I referred to legal cases because they afforded examples of real situations as against the imaginary ones normally used by economists in their analysis. It was undoubtedly an economist who invented the widget. But in 'The Problem of Social Cost' I did something else. I pointed out that the judges in their opinions often seemed to show a better understanding of the economic problem than did many economists even though their views were not always expressed in a very explicit fashion. I did this not to praise the judges but to shame economists.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

Despite wandering accidentally into law and economics, the opportunity to edit the Journal of Law and Economics was instrumental in bringing him to the University of Chicago:

> [W]hen I was approached to fill Aaron Director's place on his retirement, what I found most attractive about coming to Chicago was the opportunity it gave me of editing the Journal. Indeed, it is probable that without the Journal I would not have come to Chicago. I knew nothing of the original aim of the Journal. What I wanted to do was to encourage the type of research which I had advocated in 'The Problem of Social Cost', and I used my editorship of the Journal as a means of bringing this about.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

Coase believed that the University of Chicago was the intellectual center of law and economics. He concluded his Simons lecture by stating:

> I am very much aware that, in concentrating in this lecture on law and economics at Chicago, I have neglected other significant contributions to the subject made elsewhere such as those by Guido Calabresi at Yale, by Donald Turner at Harvard, and by others. But it can hardly be denied that in the emergence of the subject of law and economics, Chicago has played a very significant part and one of which the University can be proud.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

### Coase theorem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Coase theorem")]

In [law and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_and_economics "Law and economics"), the Coase theorem ([/ˈ k oʊ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) describes the [economic efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficiency_(economics) "Efficiency (economics)") of an economic [allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_system "Economic system") or outcome in the presence of [externalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality "Externality"). The theorem states that if trade in an externality is possible and there are sufficiently low [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_costs "Transaction costs"), bargaining will lead to a [Pareto efficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency "Pareto efficiency") outcome regardless of the initial allocation of property. In practice, obstacles to bargaining or poorly defined property rights can prevent Coasean bargaining. This 'theorem' is commonly attributed to Coase.

### Coase conjecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Coase conjecture")]

Another important contribution of Coase is the [Coase conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_conjecture "Coase conjecture"), which is an informal argument that durable goods [monopolists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") do not have market power because they are unable to commit to not lowering their prices in future periods.

## Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Political views")]

When asked what he considered his politics to be, Coase stated,

> I really don't know. I don't reject any policy without considering what its results are. If someone says there's going to be [regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_economics "Regulatory economics"), I don't say that regulation will be bad. Let's see. What we discover is that most regulation does produce, or has produced in recent times, a worse result. But I wouldn't like to say that all regulation would have this effect because one can think of circumstances in which it doesn't.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-29)

Coase admitted that early in life, he aligned himself with socialism.

> As a young man I was a Socialist. The first challenge to this belief came when, in 1931, 5 months before I took the final examinations for the B.Com. degree, I attended [Arnold Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Plant "Arnold Plant")'s seminar at the London School of Economics (LSE). He introduced me to Adam Smith's invisible hand and to the advantages of a competitive system. He also pointed out that government schemes in the economic sphere were often ill-conceived and were introduced to placate special interests. I adopted many of Plant's positions but continued to regard myself as a Socialist. That this meant holding what could be considered, and were, inconsistent positions was not unusual at that time. [Abba Lerner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abba_Lerner "Abba Lerner"), a fellow student and a fine theorist, with whom I had a very friendly relation, also believed in the virtues of a competitive system but was even more attached to Socialism than I was.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27)

[Guido Calabresi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Calabresi "Guido Calabresi") wrote that Coase's focus on transaction costs in _The Nature of the Firm_ was the result of his socialist beliefs. Reflecting on this, Coase wrote: "It is very difficult to know where one's ideas come from but for all I know he may well be right." Coase continued:

> My socialist sympathies gradually fell away and this process was accentuated as a result of being assigned in 1935 at LSE the course on the Economics of Public Utilities. I soon found out that very little was known about British public utilities and I set about making a series of historical studies on the water, gas, and electricity supply industries and of the Post Office and broadcasting. These researches taught me much about the public utility industries and they certainly made me aware of the defects of government operation of these industries, whether municipal or through nationalisation. These researches were interrupted by the war, when I joined the civil service, at first, for a short period, in the [Forestry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry_Commission "Forestry Commission"), then responsible for timber production, and for the rest of the war, in the [Central Statistical Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Statistical_Office_(United_Kingdom) "Central Statistical Office (United Kingdom)"), one of the offices of the War Cabinet. This war-time experience did not significantly influence my views but I could not help noticing that, with the country in mortal danger and despite the leadership of Winston Churchill, government departments often seemed more concerned to defend their own interests than those of the country.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27)

## Ronald Coase Institute

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Ronald Coase Institute")]

Coase was research advisor to the [Ronald Coase Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase_Institute?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ronald Coase Institute (page does not exist)"), an organisation that promotes research on institutions and organizations – the laws, rules, customs, and norms – that govern real economic systems, with particular support for young scholars from developing and transitional countries.

**Ronald Harry Coase** ([/k oʊ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); 29 December 1910 – 2 September 2013) was a British economist and author. Coase was educated at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"), where he was a member of the faculty until 1951. He was the Clifton R. Musser Professor of Economics at the [University of Chicago Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Law_School "University of Chicago Law School"), where he arrived in 1964 and remained for the rest of his life. He received the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in 1991.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-1)

Coase believed economists should study real-world wealth creation, in the manner of [Adam Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Smith "Adam Smith"), stating, "It is suicidal for the field to slide into a hard science of choice, ignoring the influences of society, history, culture, and politics on the working of the economy."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-2) He believed economic study should reduce emphasis on [price theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_theory "Price theory") or theoretical markets and instead focus on real markets.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:1-4) He established the case for the corporation as a means to pay the costs of operating a marketplace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:0-3) Coase is best known for two articles: "[The Nature of the Firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nature_of_the_Firm "The Nature of the Firm")" (1937), which introduces the concept of [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") to explain the nature and limits of [firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation"); and "[The Problem of Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Problem_of_Social_Cost "The Problem of Social Cost")" (1960), which suggests that well-defined [property rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_rights_(economics) "Property rights (economics)") could overcome the problems of [externalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externalities "Externalities") if it were not for transaction costs (see [Coase theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem "Coase theorem")). Additionally, Coase's transaction costs approach has been influential in modern [organizational economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizational_economics "Organizational economics"), where it was re-introduced by [Oliver E. Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_E._Williamson "Oliver E. Williamson").

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg/250px-Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_scan_10_edited.jpg)

Ronald Coase

Ronald Harry Coase was born in [Willesden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willesden "Willesden"), a suburb of London, on 29 December 1910. His father, Henry Joseph Coase (1884–1973) was a [telegraphist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraphist "Telegraphist") for the post office, as was his mother, Rosalie Elizabeth Coase (née Giles; 1882–1972), before marriage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-International-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-7) As a child, Coase had a weakness in his legs, for which he was required to wear [leg-irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brace_(orthopaedic) "Brace (orthopaedic)"). Due to this problem, he attended the school for physical defectives. At the age of 12, he was able to enter [Kilburn Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilburn_Grammar_School "Kilburn Grammar School") on scholarship. At Kilburn, he studied for the intermediate examination of the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") as an [external student](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London_International_Programmes "University of London International Programmes") in 1927–29.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-Coase_Autobiography-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-9)

Coase then continued his studies at the University of London, enrolling as an internal student of the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"), where he took courses with [Arnold Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Plant "Arnold Plant")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-Coase_Autobiography-8) and received a [Bachelor of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Commerce "Bachelor of Commerce") degree in 1932. During his undergraduate studies, Coase received the Sir Ernest Cassel Travelling Scholarship which he used to visit the University of Chicago in 1931–1932 studying with [Frank Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Knight "Frank Knight") and [Jacob Viner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Viner "Jacob Viner"). Coase's colleagues would later admit that they did not remember this first visit.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-FireofTruth-10) Between 1932 and 1934, Coase was an assistant lecturer at the Dundee School of Economics and Commerce, which later became part of the [University of Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Dundee "University of Dundee"). Subsequently, Coase was an assistant lecturer in commerce at the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") between 1934 and 1935 before returning to [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") as a member of staff until 1951 in which year he was awarded an earned doctorate in economics from the University of London. He then started to work at the [University at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York") and retained his British citizenship after moving to the United States in the 1950s.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-11) In 1958, he moved to the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia"). Coase settled at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") in 1964 and became the co-editor of the _[Journal of Law and Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal\_of\_Law\_and\_Economics "Journal of Law and Economics")_ with [Aaron Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Director "Aaron Director").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-12) He was also for a time a trustee of the [Philadelphia Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Society "Philadelphia Society").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-13) He received the [Nobel Prize in Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Economics "Nobel Prize in Economics") in 1991.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_%281910%E2%80%932013%29_at_Graceland_Cemetery%2C_Chicago.jpg/250px-Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_%281910%E2%80%932013%29_at_Graceland_Cemetery%2C_Chicago.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grave_of_Ronald_Coase_(1910%E2%80%932013)_at_Graceland_Cemetery,_Chicago.jpg)

Ronald Harry Coase's grave at [Graceland Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graceland_Cemetery "Graceland Cemetery"). The epitaph reads: "Here Sleeps in Peace RONALD H. COASE 1910 - 2013 Devoted husband and single-minded economist, whose ideas have inspired the great transformation of China and will continue to inspire our inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations."

Nearing his 100th birthday, Coase was working on a book concerning the rise of the economies of China and Vietnam.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-14) In an interview, Coase explained the mission of the Coase China Society and his vision of economics and the part to be played by Chinese economists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-16) This became "How China Became Capitalist" (2012) co-authored with Ning Wang. Coase was honoured and received an honorary doctorate from the university at Buffalo Department of Economics in May 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-17)

Coase married Marian Ruth Hartung of Chicago, Illinois in Willesden, England, 7 August 1937.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-International-6) Although they were unable to have children, they were married 75 years until her death on 17 October 2012, making him one of the longest-married Nobel Prize laureates.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-:1-4)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-NYT-18) Coase himself died in Chicago on 2 September 2013, at the age of 102.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-19) Both are buried at [Graceland Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graceland_Cemetery "Graceland Cemetery") in Chicago.

He was praised across the political spectrum, with _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ calling him "one of the most distinguished economists in the world"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-slate-20) and _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ calling him "the greatest of the many great University of Chicago economists".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-forbes-21)_[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ called his work over eight decades "impossible to summarize" while recommending five of his papers to read.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-wapo-22)

## Contributions to economics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contributions to economics")]

### "The Nature of the Firm"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: \"The Nature of the Firm\"")]

Main article: [The Nature of the Firm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nature_of_the_Firm "The Nature of the Firm")

In "The Nature of the Firm" (1937), a brief but highly influential essay, Coase attempts to explain why the economy features a number of [business firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation "Corporation") instead of consisting exclusively of a multitude of independent, self-employed people who contract with one another. Given that "production could be carried on without any organization [that is, firms] at all", Coase asks, why and under what conditions should we expect firms to emerge?

Since modern firms can only emerge when an entrepreneur of some sort begins to hire people, Coase's analysis proceeds by considering the conditions under which it makes sense for an entrepreneur to seek hired help instead of contracting out for some particular task.

The traditional economic theory of the time (in the tradition of [Adam Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Smith "Adam Smith")) suggested that, because the market is "efficient" (that is, those who are best at providing each good or service most cheaply are already doing so), it should always be cheaper to contract out than to hire.

Coase noted, however, a number of [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") involved in using the market; the cost of obtaining a good or service via the market actually exceeds the price of the good. Other costs, including search and information costs, bargaining costs, keeping [trade secrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_secret "Trade secret"), and policing and enforcement costs, can all potentially add to the cost of procuring something from another party. This suggests that firms will arise which can internalise the production of goods and services required to deliver a product, thus avoiding these costs. This argument sets the stage for the later contributions by [Oliver Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Williamson "Oliver Williamson"): markets and hierarchies are alternative co-ordination mechanisms for economic transactions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-24)

There is a natural limit to what a firm can produce internally, however. Coase notices "decreasing returns to the entrepreneur function", including increasing [overhead costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_expenses "Overhead expenses") and increasing propensity for an overwhelmed manager to make mistakes in resource allocation. These factors become countervailing costs to the use of the firm.

Coase argues that the size of a firm (as measured by how many contractual relations are "internal" to the firm and how many "external") is a result of finding an optimal balance between the competing tendencies of the costs outlined above. In general, making the firm larger will initially be advantageous, but the decreasing returns indicated above will eventually kick in, preventing the firm from growing indefinitely.

Other things being equal, therefore, a firm will tend to be larger:

*   the lower the costs of organising and the slower these costs rise with an increase in the number of transactions organised
*   the less likely the entrepreneur is to make mistakes and the smaller the increase in mistakes with an increase in the transactions organised
*   the greater the lowering (or the smaller the rise) in the supply price of factors of production to firms of larger size

The first two costs will increase with the spatial distribution of the transactions organised and the dissimilarity of the transactions. This explains why firms tend to either be in different geographic locations or to perform different functions. Additionally, technology changes that mitigate the cost of organising transactions across space may allow firms to become larger – the advent of the telephone and of cheap air travel, for example, would be expected to increase the size of firms.

A further exploration of the dichotomy between markets and hierarchies as co-ordination mechanisms for economic transactions derived a third alternative way called [Commons based peer production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commons_based_peer_production "Commons based peer production"), in which individuals successfully collaborate on large-scale projects following a diverse cluster of motivational drives and social signals.

### "The Problem of Social Cost"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"The Problem of Social Cost\"")]

Main article: [The Problem of Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Problem_of_Social_Cost "The Problem of Social Cost")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Coase_working_2000s.jpg/250px-Coase_working_2000s.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_working_2000s.jpg)

Coase at the University of Chicago Law School in 2003

Upon publishing his article The Federal Communications Commission in 1959, Coase received negative feedback from the faculty at the University of Chicago over his conclusions and apparent conflicts with [A.C. Pigou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Cecil_Pigou "Arthur Cecil Pigou"). According to Coase, "What I said was thought to run counter to Pigou's analysis by a number of economists at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") and was therefore, according to them, wrong. At a meeting in Chicago I was able to convince these economists that I was right and Pigou's analysis faulty." Coase had presented his paper in 1960 during a seminar in Chicago, to twenty senior economist including [George Stigler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stigler "George Stigler") and [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman "Milton Friedman"). He gradually won over the usually skeptic audience, in what has later been considered a "paradigm-shifting moment" in the genesis of Chicago Law and Economics.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-25) Coase would join the Chicago faculty four years later.

Published in the _Journal of Law and Economics_ in 1960, while Coase was a member of the Economics department at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia"), "The Problem of [Social Cost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Cost "Social Cost")" provided the key insight that it is unclear where the blame for externalities lies. The example he gave was of a rancher whose cattle stray onto the cropland of his neighbour. If the rancher is made to restrict his cattle, he is harmed just as the farmer is if the cattle remain unrestrained.

Coase argued that without [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_cost "Transaction cost") the initial assignment of property rights makes no difference to whether or not the farmer and rancher can achieve the economically efficient outcome. If the cost of restraining cattle by, say, building a fence, is less than the cost of crop damage, the fence will be built. The initial assignment of property rights determines who builds the fence. If the farmer is responsible for the crop damage, the farmer will pay for the fence (as long the fence costs less than the crop damage). The allocation of property rights is primarily an equity issue, with consequences for the distribution of income and wealth, rather than an efficiency issue.

With sufficient transaction costs, initial property rights matter for both equity and efficiency. From the point of view of economic efficiency, property rights should be assigned such that the owner of the rights wants to take the economically efficient action. To elaborate, if it is efficient not to restrict the cattle, the rancher should be given the rights (so that cattle can move about freely), whereas if it is efficient to restrict the cattle, the farmer should be given the rights over the movement of the cattle (so the cattle are restricted).

This seminal argument forms the basis of the famous [Coase theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_theorem "Coase theorem") as labelled by Stigler. In 1990, Coase wrote that he feared "The Problem of Social Cost" had been widely misunderstood.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-26)

### Law and economics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Law and economics")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Coase_profile_2003.jpg/250px-Coase_profile_2003.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coase_profile_2003.jpg)

Coase at the University of Chicago Law School

Though trained as an economist, Coase spent much of his career working in a law school. He is a central figure in the development of the subfield of [law and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_and_economics "Law and economics"). He viewed law and economics as having two parts, the first "using the economists' approach and concepts to analyze the working of the legal system, often called the economic analysis of the law"; and the second "a study of the influence of the legal system on the working of the economic system."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27) Coase said that the second part "is the part of law and economics in which I am most interested."

In his Simons Lecture celebrating the centennial of the University of Chicago, titled "Law and Economics at Chicago", Coase noted that he only accidentally wandered into the field:

> It is generally agreed that this article has had an immense influence on legal scholarship, but this was no part of my intention. For me, 'The Problem of Social Cost' was an essay in economics. It was aimed at economists. What I wanted to do was to improve our analysis of the working of the economic system. Law came into article because, in a regime of positive transaction costs, the character of the law becomes one of the main factors determining the performance of the economy. If transaction costs were zero (as is assumed in standard economic theory) we can imagine people contracting around the law whenever the value of production would be increased by a change in the legal position. But in a regime of positive transaction costs, such contracting would not occur whenever transaction costs were greater than the gain that such a redistribution of rights would bring. As a consequence the rights which individuals possess will commonly be those established by the law, which in these circumstances can be said to control the economy. As I have said, in 'The Problem of Social Cost' I had no intention of making a contribution to legal scholarship. I referred to legal cases because they afforded examples of real situations as against the imaginary ones normally used by economists in their analysis. It was undoubtedly an economist who invented the widget. But in 'The Problem of Social Cost' I did something else. I pointed out that the judges in their opinions often seemed to show a better understanding of the economic problem than did many economists even though their views were not always expressed in a very explicit fashion. I did this not to praise the judges but to shame economists.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

Despite wandering accidentally into law and economics, the opportunity to edit the Journal of Law and Economics was instrumental in bringing him to the University of Chicago:

> [W]hen I was approached to fill Aaron Director's place on his retirement, what I found most attractive about coming to Chicago was the opportunity it gave me of editing the Journal. Indeed, it is probable that without the Journal I would not have come to Chicago. I knew nothing of the original aim of the Journal. What I wanted to do was to encourage the type of research which I had advocated in 'The Problem of Social Cost', and I used my editorship of the Journal as a means of bringing this about.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

Coase believed that the University of Chicago was the intellectual center of law and economics. He concluded his Simons lecture by stating:

> I am very much aware that, in concentrating in this lecture on law and economics at Chicago, I have neglected other significant contributions to the subject made elsewhere such as those by Guido Calabresi at Yale, by Donald Turner at Harvard, and by others. But it can hardly be denied that in the emergence of the subject of law and economics, Chicago has played a very significant part and one of which the University can be proud.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LEChicago-28)

### Coase theorem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Coase theorem")]

In [law and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_and_economics "Law and economics"), the Coase theorem ([/ˈ k oʊ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) describes the [economic efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficiency_(economics) "Efficiency (economics)") of an economic [allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_system "Economic system") or outcome in the presence of [externalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Externality "Externality"). The theorem states that if trade in an externality is possible and there are sufficiently low [transaction costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaction_costs "Transaction costs"), bargaining will lead to a [Pareto efficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency "Pareto efficiency") outcome regardless of the initial allocation of property. In practice, obstacles to bargaining or poorly defined property rights can prevent Coasean bargaining. This 'theorem' is commonly attributed to Coase.

### Coase conjecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Coase conjecture")]

Another important contribution of Coase is the [Coase conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coase_conjecture "Coase conjecture"), which is an informal argument that durable goods [monopolists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") do not have market power because they are unable to commit to not lowering their prices in future periods.

## Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Political views")]

When asked what he considered his politics to be, Coase stated,

> I really don't know. I don't reject any policy without considering what its results are. If someone says there's going to be [regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulatory_economics "Regulatory economics"), I don't say that regulation will be bad. Let's see. What we discover is that most regulation does produce, or has produced in recent times, a worse result. But I wouldn't like to say that all regulation would have this effect because one can think of circumstances in which it doesn't.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-29)

Coase admitted that early in life, he aligned himself with socialism.

> As a young man I was a Socialist. The first challenge to this belief came when, in 1931, 5 months before I took the final examinations for the B.Com. degree, I attended [Arnold Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Plant "Arnold Plant")'s seminar at the London School of Economics (LSE). He introduced me to Adam Smith's invisible hand and to the advantages of a competitive system. He also pointed out that government schemes in the economic sphere were often ill-conceived and were introduced to placate special interests. I adopted many of Plant's positions but continued to regard myself as a Socialist. That this meant holding what could be considered, and were, inconsistent positions was not unusual at that time. [Abba Lerner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abba_Lerner "Abba Lerner"), a fellow student and a fine theorist, with whom I had a very friendly relation, also believed in the virtues of a competitive system but was even more attached to Socialism than I was.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27)

[Guido Calabresi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Calabresi "Guido Calabresi") wrote that Coase's focus on transaction costs in _The Nature of the Firm_ was the result of his socialist beliefs. Reflecting on this, Coase wrote: "It is very difficult to know where one's ideas come from but for all I know he may well be right." Coase continued:

> My socialist sympathies gradually fell away and this process was accentuated as a result of being assigned in 1935 at LSE the course on the Economics of Public Utilities. I soon found out that very little was known about British public utilities and I set about making a series of historical studies on the water, gas, and electricity supply industries and of the Post Office and broadcasting. These researches taught me much about the public utility industries and they certainly made me aware of the defects of government operation of these industries, whether municipal or through nationalisation. These researches were interrupted by the war, when I joined the civil service, at first, for a short period, in the [Forestry Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry_Commission "Forestry Commission"), then responsible for timber production, and for the rest of the war, in the [Central Statistical Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Statistical_Office_(United_Kingdom) "Central Statistical Office (United Kingdom)"), one of the offices of the War Cabinet. This war-time experience did not significantly influence my views but I could not help noticing that, with the country in mortal danger and despite the leadership of Winston Churchill, government departments often seemed more concerned to defend their own interests than those of the country.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase#cite_note-LESimpson-27)

## Ronald Coase Institute

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ronald_Coase&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Ronald Coase Institute")]

Coase was research advisor to the [Ronald Coase Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Coase_Institute?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ronald Coase Institute (page does not exist)"), an organisation that promotes research on institutions and organizations – the laws, rules, customs, and norms – that govern real economic systems, with particular support for young scholars from developing and transitional countries.
